document.title: The book around five projects (plan, packets book-5, book-14 and book-22)
document.p: Internal: this file is not part of the book. It plans the rewrite of docs/book that the owner asked for on 2026-10-21 ():

quote.p: restructure the content of the book around useful examples instead of the current ones: 1. keeping structured specifications for projects using XML (think IETF-style RFCs, without needing an LLM to edit large text), 2. creating and transforming SVG (e.g. a diagramming tool), 3. annotating SCXML files with data schemas and XHTML for self-describing machines, 4. using the tree-sitter bridge to create a diff of call chains, 5. recording OTel traces before and after a change and rendering a trace diff for changes in cardinality and communication participants.

document.p: The book keeps 's rules: The Rust Programming Language's style (teach by running small, real examples; no phases, packets or decision numbers in the text), every console block checked by tools/check-book-examples.sh, <!-- examples: NAME -->, <!-- requires: javascript --> and <!-- status: draft --> as today. The library/loans data goes away everywhere except Chapter 18 (codegen), which is already a project and stays as it is (until book-22: it now generates Vane's SDK clients, section 9).

section.title: 1. One story, five projects
section.p: All five projects belong to one small, made-up system, Vane: a feature-flag product (since book-22, section 9). Vane is one service, vane, a TypeScript program on Node.js whose parts are modules, not services: api (the HTTP entry points), flags (what each request does), registry (flags, targeting rules and percentages in PostgreSQL), cache (flags read recently, in Redis), rollout (the lifecycle machine of each flag, guardrail checks, the automatic pause) and audit (the audit log in PostgreSQL and the owners' webhook). It offers an evaluation API to the SDKs and an admin API to its console, both as remote functions (GET /api/getFlags, POST /api/killFlag, ...), and an update stream on which it sends a line per change. Two SDKs call it: @vane/browser, the frontend SDK, asks the service whether each flag is on for one user (evaluateFlags); @vane/node, the backend SDK, downloads every flag with its rules (getFlags), evaluates them locally, keeps them in a cache and keeps the cache current from the update stream. Owners roll flags out by percentage in the console; the service checks guardrail metrics before each step, pauses a flag after three failed checks, and has a kill switch; every change goes to the audit log. Every developer has met this, and the parts are where a real product has them. The reader meets one domain and sees the projects feed each other:

row.cell: The Vane protocol as an Internet-Draft in XML: indexes of requirements and terms, checks, targeted edits, HTML and RFC-style text
A small diagramming tool: a graph description, a computed layout, SVG written by XQuery and XSLT, SVG transformed
A flag's rollout lifecycle as an SCXML machine whose data and events carry XSD types and whose states carry XHTML documentation; checks and generated documentation
The flag service's TypeScript before and after a change, its call graph, and the diff of its call chains
OTLP JSON traces of the same change before and after, and the diff of cardinalities and participants, rendered as HTML and SVG
Vane's API as XSD types and remote functions; generated SDK clients for the browser and Node.js, the service's request validation and an OpenAPI document

section.p: The links between projects are real and small: the machine's vane:implements attributes name the draft's requirement anchors; the machine's numbers (3 failed checks, 600 s rollout steps, a 300 s pause) are the draft's; the code change of call-chains is the change the traces record; the diagram vocabulary of svg draws the system, the machine, the call-chain diff and the trace diff; the codegen project generates the SDK clients and request checks of the API that the traces record. The book says once, early (introduction), that the projects share a story, and each project chapter can be read on its own.

The story replaced an earlier one, Latch (door locks, a controller and its services), on the owner's request (2026-10-21: "nobody thinks of doors"). Book-14 rewrote the seed data with the same structure; section 8 has the rename table and the packets that carry the chapters over. Then the owner found Vane as a set of services nonsensical ("make it a monolithic service that's fully featured, and we want to offer client libraries/SDKs for frontend and backend"): book-22 made it one service and two SDKs, with the same teaching structure; section 9 has the change table and packets book-23 to book-29. Sections 3 to 7 below still use the Latch names where they describe chapter content, and section 2's spec and scxml parts keep book-14's text: read them through the tables of sections 8 and 9.

section.title: spec: an Internet-Draft in a subset of xml2rfc v3
section.p: spec/vane.xml (draft -01, draft-example-vane-protocol-01, "The Vane Protocol for Feature Flag Rollouts") and spec/vane-00.xml (the earlier draft), spec/vane.xsd.

item.p: Vocabulary: a subset of xml2rfc version 3 (RFC 7991 and the RFC Editor's current v3 grammar), no namespace, xml2rfc's element names and meanings: rfc (version, category, ipr, submissionType, docName), front (title, seriesInfo, author with organization and address/email, date, area, keyword, abstract), middle with nested section (anchor, name, t, dl/dt/dd, sourcecode), inline xref, bcp14, em, strong, tt, cref, and back with nested references and reference. Chosen over an own vocabulary because it is what IETF authors write, xml2rfc can render the file, and the book can say so.

Sections (anchors): Introduction (intro) with Terminology (terminology), Flag States (states), Messages (messages, with the ABNF) with Rollout (rollout) and Status (), Pause (pause), Security Considerations (security), IANA Considerations (iana).

Requirements are paragraphs t with an anchor holding bcp14 keywords (11 in -01: MUST 5, MUST NOT 1, SHOULD 2, SHOULD NOT 1, MAY 2; plus one unanchored SHOULD in Security Considerations, "carry Vane over an encrypted link", that cref issue-2 flags, deliberately: the "add a requirement" edit gives it an anchor). Anchors are names given once in the order written (req-1…req-11, not in document order: -01 inserted req-9, req-10, req-11 into existing sections; the document order is req-1 2 3 4 5 9 6 10 7 8 11); the renderer numbers sections and requirements by position. The requirements:

row.cell: a flag is in exactly one of "stable", "rolling-out", "paused"
a rolling-out flag returns to "stable" ten minutes after its step began
the service checks the guardrail metrics before it applies a percentage
no rollout during a pause (xref to section pause)
ask an owner for a one-time password (RFC 6238) before a rollout (-01)
answer a status request with the state and the failed checks
an SDK sends at most one status request per second per flag (-01)
three failed checks in a row pause the flag (-00: five)
a pause lasts five minutes (-00: one minute); cref issue-1
report a pause to the flag's owners (-01)

item.p: Terms are the dts of section 1.1 with anchors term-flag (Flag), term-sdk (SDK), term-percentage (Percentage), term-pause (Pause), used through <xref target="term-…">text</xref>; the Pause dd refers to term-flag. References: RFC 2119, 5234, 8174 (normative), RFC 6238 (informative, new in -01; kept from Latch because a second factor before a production rollout is plausible, and its authors, M'Raihi among them, carry the collation and array lessons of Chapters 2 and 13). One ABNF sourcecode (name="vane.abnf", for the iXML task):
item.pre: message = rollout-request / kill-request / status-request rollout-request = "ROLLOUT" SP flag-key SP percentage CRLF kill-request = "KILL" SP flag-key CRLF status-request = "STATUS" SP flag-key CRLF flag-key = 1*32(ALPHA / DIGIT / "-") percentage = 1*3DIGIT
item.p: (undefined core rules: SP, CRLF, ALPHA, DIGIT). Two cref editorial notes. Words for the full-text lessons: "flag"/"flags", "pause"/ "paused", "roll out"/"rollout"/"rolling-out", "SDK", "service", "owner"/"owners"; req-7 says "three", for format-integer(3, "w").

-00 vs -01: -01 adds req-9 (one-time password, with the RFC 6238 reference and the informative references section), req-10 (status rate) and req-11 (pause report), changes req-7 ("five" to "three" failed checks) and req-8 ("one minute" to "five minutes"), the dates (2026-07-06 to 2026-10-21), the names, and adds the leading comment. Anchors of unchanged requirements are the same, so a diff by anchor works.

book-22 changes (both drafts; the counts, anchors, keywords, the unanchored SHOULD and the -00/-01 differences are unchanged): the abstract and the introduction describe the protocol between the SDKs and "the Vane service" (no "evaluation service", no "line-based"): an SDK keeps the flags in a cache, evaluates them for each user, holds an update stream open on which the service sends a message per change, and asks for the status of a flag; the SDK term is "The library in an application that evaluates flags from its cache and keeps the cache current with Vane messages"; the Percentage term adds the rollout semantics ("An SDK puts a user in the share by a hash of the flag and the user, so the user stays in it while the percentage grows"); the Messages paragraph says the lines travel on the update stream (the service sends ROLLOUT and KILL, an SDK sends STATUS); the ABNF rules are rollout-update, kill-update, status-request (same shape: six rules, the same references, the same undefined core rules); req-10 (-01) ends "; it uses its cached answer in between" (the SDK caching rule; 22 words); Security begins "Vane messages travel in clear text on the network." The ABNF is now:
item.pre: message = rollout-update / kill-update / status-request rollout-update = "ROLLOUT" SP flag-key SP percentage CRLF kill-update = "KILL" SP flag-key CRLF status-request = "STATUS" SP flag-key CRLF flag-key = 1*32(ALPHA / DIGIT / "-") percentage = 1*3DIGIT

item.p: vane.xsd (XSD 1.1, vc:minVersion="1.1"), latch.xsd unchanged but its comment: named simple types (anchor, draft-name with a pattern, enumerating BCP 14's eleven levels with an annotation, month, day), mixed content (text), a group of inline elements, xs:simpleContent extensions (title, sourcecode), recursive section and references, an xs:assert (docName equals the Internet-Draft seriesInfo), xs:unique over all anchors (not xs:key: most paragraphs have none) and an xs:keyref from xref/@target.

section.title: svg: a diagram description and its drawing
section.p: svg/diagram.xml, svg/diagram.svg.

item.p: Vocabulary (own, no namespace): diagram (title) with (id, label, optional kind="store") and edge (from, to, optional label), and the optional class on node and edge (copied to the SVG group, so a diff can colour added, removed, changed). Unchanged by book-22.

The diagram ("Vane", book-22): the two SDKs, the modules of the one service as boxes labelled vane/MODULE, and the two stores. Nodes browser (@vane/browser), (@vane/node), api (vane/api), flags (vane/flags), registry (vane/registry), cache (vane/cache), postgresql (store), redis (store); edges browser→api HTTP, node→api HTTP, api→flags, flags→registry, flags→cache (module calls have no label), registry→postgresql SQL, cache→redis Redis. The console, the rollout and audit modules are not drawn (the audit module appears only after the change, in the chapter's change.xml). Modules are boxes, not a grouped box: the vocabulary and the layout code stay as they are, and the vane/ prefix says that the boxes are parts of one program (a group element would be new layout machinery for one picture).

diagram.svg is the drawing the svg chapter's code makes (draw.xq writes it byte for byte; book-22 regenerated it with the committed draw.xq and draw.xqm, unchanged), with this layout: rank of a node = breadth-first distance from the nodes without incoming edges (cycles allowed; for this DAG equal to the longest path); one row per rank, top to bottom, nodes in document order, each row centred; boxes 140 x 40, gaps 40 across and 60 down, padding 20, so width = 2·20 + n·140 + (n−1)·40 for the widest row; five ranks (browser node / api / flags / registry cache / postgresql redis), 360 x 480; edges are lines from the bottom centre of the source to the top centre of the target with an arrow marker, the label at the midpoint (+6, +4) when there is one; services rect rx="6", stores rx="20"; a style element with five rules; ids node-ID, edge-FROM-TO; edges drawn before nodes. The file is the serialization with indent=yes of the SVG namespace as the default namespace. The ids node-flags and node-cache remain (svg-xslt.md uses them).

section.title: scxml: a feature flag that describes itself
section.p: scxml/flag.scxml, scxml/scxml.xsd, scxml/vane-data.xsd.

item.p: Machine feature_flag (SCXML 1.0 namespace, datamodel="ecmascript"), one flag's rollout lifecycle: states stable (initial: the flag keeps its percentage), checking (the guardrail metrics are checked), rolling-out (the new percentage is served for one step), paused (rollouts refused), archived. Transitions: stable --rollout.request--> checking; stable status.request (targetless, send status.response); checking --check.passed--> rolling-out (assign failures 0); checking --check.failed, cond failures + 1 < maxFailures--> stable (assign failures + 1); checking --check.failed--> paused; rolling-out (onentry: send step.done with delayexpr) --"kill.request step.done"--> stable (two events in one attribute); rolling-out flag.evaluated (targetless, log); paused (onentry: send pause.expired) --pause.expired--> stable (assign failures 0); archived --kill.request--> stable. The same graph as the Latch machine (locked, checking, unlocked, lockout, jammed).

Self-description, in the namespace urn:example:vane: vane:events declares nine events (vane:event name, optional vane:payload naming a payload element of vane-data.xsd, and an XHTML p): rollout.request (payload vane:rollout), check.passed, check.failed, kill.request, status.request, status.response (payload vane:status), step.done, pause.expired, flag.archived. Data: failures 0 (vane:failure-count), maxFailures 3 (vane:failure-limit), stepSeconds 600 and pauseSeconds 300 (vane:seconds). vane:implements: stable req-2, the status transition req-6, checking req-4, the check.failed → paused transition req-7, rolling-out req-3, paused "req-5 req-8"; each state has an XHTML div (rolling-out and paused with a var).

Deliberate flaws, valid against the schemas, found by the schema-aware checks of Chapter 7: archived is unreachable (no transition targets it), flag.evaluated is handled but not declared, flag.archived is declared but neither handled nor sent (the author forgot the archive transition: the fix adds it), and status.response is only sent (a check must count send/@event as used, or report it as outgoing). The draft's only MUST that nothing implements is req-1.

scxml.xsd: unchanged but for its comment and the import (xs:import of vane-data.xsd for urn:example:vane): a subset of the Recommendation's schema (one target per transition, so a keyref can check it; four executable elements), lax xs:any and xs:anyAttribute ##other, two xs:asserts citing SCXML 1.0 3.5 and 5.3.1, xs:key state-id with keyrefs for targets and initial.

vane-data.xsd: simple types with facets (failure-count, failure-limit ≤ 10, seconds ≤ 3600, flag-key and percentage patterns matching the draft's ABNF — [A-Za-z0-9\-]{1,32} and [0-9]{1,3}, so the pattern, like the ABNF, allows 999: a facet lesson —, state enumeration stable, rolling-out, paused), xs:documentation on seconds, flag-key and percentage (the request under "Proposed data changes"), payload elements rollout (flag, percentage, optional owner) and (flag, state, failed-checks, optional retry-after, with an xs:assert tying retry-after to the state paused), global attributes type, payload, implements (an xs:list), the events element with xs:unique on names, and vane:value of type xs:anySimpleType, so that a query can check a data value against its type with xsi:type.

section.title: call-chains: a TypeScript service, before and after
section.p: call-chains/before/{api,flags,registry,cache,db}.ts, call-chains/after/{api,flags,registry,audit,db}.ts (book-22; TypeScript, built in; namespace imports import * as registry from "./registry.ts" make callees module-qualified). They are a cut of the Vane service: the modules on the path of the two remote functions the change touches.

item.p: api.ts (was server.ts): route answers GET /api/getFlags (listFlags, the flags with their rules that the backend SDK downloads; the answer is { flags }) and POST /api/killFlag (body { flag, owner }, killFlag, the kill switch of the admin API that the console calls; the answer is { flag, killed }), else { problems: ["no function …"] }; start with createServer and an arrow function, so the call graph attributes the calls to the enclosing named function. The routes are the remote functions of the codegen project's api.xml.

db.ts (was http.ts): the Rule and Flag interfaces (Flag: key, name, state, percentage, rules, owners) and query(text, values) over a pg.Pool (pool.query is external). Calls carry no type arguments (await query<Flag>(…) parses as a call of await query, an ERROR-free but wrong tree in tree-sitter-typescript); callers cast with as.

registry.ts: getFlags (SELECT key, name, state, percentage, rules, owners FROM flags), getFlag(key) (… WHERE key = $1), setPercentage(key, percentage) (UPDATE flags SET percentage = $2 WHERE key = $1); after: getFlagKeys (SELECT key FROM flags) instead of getFlags.
cache.ts (before only): getFlag(key) reads flag:${key} from Redis (redis://redis:6379).
flags.ts: FlagSummary is what an SDK needs to evaluate a flag (key, state, percentage, rules: no name, no owners); summarize destructures its parameter; listFlags, isOwner, killFlag.
audit.ts (after only): record(flagKey, action) inserts into audit_events (flag, action) through db.query and posts to the owners' webhook https://hooks.example.com/vane with fetch.

section.p: The change (vane 2.3.0 to 2.4.0), in flags.ts: listFlags called registry.getFlags() once; now it calls registry.getFlagKeys() and then registry.getFlag(key) in a for … of loop (an N+1 against the database; a static check sees the call inside a loop); killFlag no longer reads cache.getFlag (a kill must read the flag from the database, not from a cache that may be a minute old; cache.ts is gone) and now calls audit.record(key, "kill") (audit.ts is new). Function counts per file: api 2, cache 1, db 1, flags 4, registry 3, audit 1. Chains (chains.xq): api.start > api.route > flags.listFlags > registry.getFlags > db.query before; after, … > registry.getFlag* > db.query and … > flags.killFlag > audit.record > db.query.
call-chains/kinds/flag.ts and the chapter's code are not seeds; the chapter's graph.xqm, chains.xq, diff.xq and report.xq ran unchanged on the new files.

section.title: traces: OTLP JSON before and after
section.p: traces/before.json (14 spans), traces/after.json (23 spans), each an OTLP ExportTraceServiceRequest in JSON (the OTLP/HTTP JSON encoding: hex trace and span ids, kind as an integer, times as decimal strings, intValue as a string), as a collector writes them: resourceSpans per process (service.name, service.version, deployment.environment.name staging), scopeSpans per instrumentation library. Written by book-22 (the generator script is not committed; trace ids and start times are book-14's, span ids are new). Two traces per file:

item.p: GET /api/getFlags (09:00:00.000): the backend SDK refreshes its flags. Root: a client span in resource storefront 5.2.0 (an application that embeds the SDK), scope @vane/node 1.4.0, server.address vane, url.template /api/getFlags. Then in resource vane: the server span (scope @opentelemetry/instrumentation-http, http.route), internal spans per module function (kind 1, scope vane with the service's version, named after the function: flags.listFlags, registry.getFlags, code.function.name, and vane.flag.key where a flag is meant), and PostgreSQL client spans (scope @opentelemetry/instrumentation-pg, db.system.name postgresql, db.operation.name, db.collection.name, db.query.text as the code writes it, server.address postgresql, port 5432).

POST /api/killFlag (09:00:02.000): an owner pulls the kill switch of new-checkout. Root: a client span in resource vane-console 1.8.0 (the console in a browser, scope @opentelemetry/instrumentation-fetch, server.address vane.example.com); the server span; flags.killFlag; before: cache.getFlag with a Redis client span (GET, db.system.name redis, GET flag:new-checkout, server.address redis), then registry.getFlag with SELECT flags, and registry.setPercentage with UPDATE flags; after: no cache, audit.record with INSERT audit_events and the webhook, a client span POST (scope @opentelemetry/instrumentation-undici, server.address hooks.example.com, url.full https://hooks.example.com/vane) with no server span.

section.p: Participants come from client spans: the service of the server span whose parent is the client span, else server.address (postgresql, redis and hooks.example.com have no server spans). Internal spans are not calls. The diff (the traces chapter's diff.xq, unchanged, run on the new files):
section.pre: vane: 2.3.0 -> 2.4.0 GET /api/getFlags: vane -> postgresql 1 -> 5 POST /api/killFlag: vane -> hooks.example.com 0 -> 1 POST /api/killFlag: vane -> postgresql 2 -> 3 POST /api/killFlag: vane -> redis 1 -> 0
section.p: The new participant is the owners' webhook (hooks.example.com); the N+1 is a run of four registry.getFlag internal spans (each with a SELECT flags) under flags.listFlags, for new-checkout, dark-mode, fast-search, beta-banner; the removed call is Redis; the audit write raises the kill's PostgreSQL calls from 2 to 3. There is no "none ->" version line any more: nothing new has a resource of its own (the storefront and the console keep their versions). The participants diagram of participants.xq draws a callee without a resource as a store, which is wrong for the webhook: the traces packet decides (for example, a store only when the client span has db.system.name).

item.p: Project directories are example directories. A chapter file that uses a project names that project's directory: <!-- examples: spec -->. The reader runs every command of a project from one directory, like a real repository. Chapters that use no project keep their own directory (getting-started, ixml, source-code, c, javascript, codegen).

Seed files are frozen during the rewrite. The files of section 2 are read-only for every packet. A packet that needs a change writes it under "Proposed data changes" at the end of this file and goes on without it; the integration packet decides. (The svg packet may regenerate diagram.svg from its own code, as said above; it is the only exception, and it then runs every chapter that shows that file.)

New files in a shared directory are owned by the packet that adds them. Before adding a name, git ls-files docs/book/examples/DIR and the "Files" list of the other packets below; never take a name another packet lists. Never list a project directory's root in an example (file:list("."), ls): other packets add files there. A packet that needs a listing makes a subdirectory of its own.

Cross-project files are relative symlinks to seed files (or to a file another packet has committed, which is then an order constraint), committed in the using directory by the using packet, e.g. scxml/latch.xml -> ../spec/latch.xml. check-book-examples.sh copies directories with shutil.copytree, which follows symlinks, and {{#include}} should name the target's real path.

SUMMARY.md, introduction.md, foreword.md and the appendices belong to the integration packet (book-13). A rewrite packet checks its files with tools/check-book-examples.sh BUILD file.md… (which does not need SUMMARY) and lists any new glossary term for book-13 in its final report. New chapter files are not in SUMMARY until book-13; mdBook ignores them meanwhile. Run mdbook build only after book-13.
Cross references: refer to other chapters by title with a link ([Transforming with XSLT](xslt.md)), not by number: the numbers move. book-13 replaces the remaining "Chapter N" texts (37 today).
Old example directories are deleted by the packet that takes over their chapters, in the commit that stops using them (see each packet).

Every feature in the coverage table (section 6) is taught where the table says, with at least the depth the old chapter had; a packet that cannot (an sxml limit), keeps the old text's point with the new data and says so in its report.

Each packet: release build of a HEAD snapshot (one at a time, deleted at the end), the check on its chapter files, a LOG entry, a decision record only for choices the next packets need, commit and push at each finished chapter. The book never mentions packets, phases or decisions.

section.title: 5. The chapters
section.p: For each file: the project directory (its examples: comment), what it teaches in order, the main files it adds, and the packet. "Seed" means the files of section 2.

section.title: 1. Getting Started (book-6) — examples: getting-started
section.p: Stays tiny and self-contained: getting-started/draft.xml, a ten-line cut of the draft (two sections, three requirements); draft.xsd; broken.xml; invalid.xml (a bcp14 of "MIGHT" and a missing name); requirements.xq; outline.xsl. installation.md is unchanged except its "Following along" paragraph. hello-xpath.md: strings, //t, string(), predicates (//t[bcp14 = "MUST"]), count, @anchor, !, the two errors. the-sxml-command.md: check, validate, xquery, transform, serialize, exit status, as today. Replaces books.xml and friends.

section.title: 2. Finding Things with XPath (book-6) — examples: spec

item.p: xpath.md: what an expression is; the draft as a tree (front, middle, sections, mixed content of t).

xpath-paths.md: steps from the top (/rfc/middle/section/name), predicates (section[@anchor = "lockout"]), positions (section[2], (//t[bcp14])[last()]), axes (ancestor::section for "which section is this requirement in", following-sibling, preceding, the section number as count(preceding-sibling::section) + 1 per ancestor), kinds of nodes (text(), comment, processing-instruction, the cref), combining (|, except: requirements outside Security), the value of a node (string(t) across xref and bcp14).

xpath-values.md: literals, arithmetic (counting requirements per keyword), untyped values (@year of references: RFC 2119 1997), general vs value comparison (bcp14 = ("MUST", "SHALL")), dates (xs:date from date/@year/@month/@day with a month map; the age of each reference; durations between -00 and -01: doc("latch-00.xml")), effective boolean values, sequence types.

xpath-functions.md: strings (normalize-space of paragraphs, the docName's version with substring-after/tokenize), regular expressions (finding BCP 14 words written without bcp14 markup: matches(., "\b(MUST|SHOULD|MAY)\b") in text nodes, a classic draft bug), numbers (format-number of percentages per keyword), sequences (distinct-values of keywords, index-of), the arrow operator, conditions (if, otherwise), variables and loops (let, for in XPath), namespaces of functions.

xpath-maps-arrays.md: maps (anchor to title: the lookup table for xrefs), maps from documents (map:merge(//*[@anchor] ! {@anchor: …})), arrays (the authors of each reference as arrays), JSON (the requirement list serialized with method json and read back with parse-json), records (record(anchor, keyword, section)).

xpath-higher-order.md: inline functions, named references, partial application, sort-by (requirements by keyword strength: a map from keyword to rank), filter/for-each/fold-left (the requirement count per section), functions that make functions (a checker per keyword), what XPath can't do alone (points to XQuery).

section.p: Deletes examples/xpath/ with its last use.

section.title: 3. Writing Programs with XQuery (book-7) — examples: spec

item.p: xquery.md: running a query file against the draft; comments; the chapter's plan.

xquery-flwor.md: for/where/order by/return (the requirements index), let, positions (at), joins (xrefs to terms joined with the dts; requirements of -00 with those of -01 by anchor), group by (first look), count, while (the requirements before the first SHOULD), more clauses.

xquery-grouping.md: grouping by a computed key (the section of each requirement), several keys (section and keyword), after the grouping (counts, string-join), choosing a key well. Ends with one paragraph that points to windows in Who Calls Whom, and How Often.

xquery-constructors.md: direct constructors (an XHTML index of requirements), enclosed expressions, computed constructors (an element named after the keyword), namespaces (the XHTML namespace, the default element namespace), not only XML (text, comments, processing instructions; maps).

xquery-types-errors.md: switch (keyword to strength), typeswitch (block kinds t, dl, sourcecode), saying what you expect (as), naming types (declare type keyword as enum(…)), kinds of errors, try/catch (a check that reports every xref to a missing anchor without stopping), raising errors (error(xs:QName("spec:dangling"), …)), errors on purpose (finally).

xquery-modules.md: spec.xqm (namespace urn:example:spec): spec:requirements($doc), spec:section-number($section), spec:keywords($t), spec:anchor-map($doc); library modules, external variables ($draft), typed functions catching mistakes, private functions and module variables, functions as values, a failed import.

xquery-inputs.md: the context item, doc(), many documents (both drafts and, after cli-3, collection() over a drafts/ subdirectory book-7 adds), external variables (--param=draft=latch-00.xml). Order: after cli-3's commit, which edits this file today.

xquery-serialization.md: output methods; the requirements index as XML, XHTML, HTML (method=html), JSON (an array of records), CSV (anchor, section, keyword, text), text; serialize() inside a query; saving with --output.

xquery-updates.md: on draft -01: give the unanchored SHOULD an anchor (insert node attribute anchor {…}) and remove issue-2's cref; add a requirement after req-8 (insert node … after); rename a term everywhere (dt, every xref to it and its text: one pending update list); move a section and see that nothing needs renumbering; renumber requirement anchors in document order and every xref with them (and the warning: other documents, such as lock.scxml, refer to anchors); copy-modify, transform with; updating functions; the errors XUST0001, XUTY0005, XUDY0015; fn:put of draft -02.
xquery-4.md: as today, examples over the draft.

xquery-project.md, Project: Editing a Specification Without Rewriting It: edit.xqm (updating functions: add-requirement, rename-term, set-keyword, add-reference), check.xq (dangling xrefs, unused terms and references, BCP 14 words without markup, requirements without anchors; exit with an error code), changes.xq (the requirement diff -00 to -01: added, removed, changed text, changed keyword; as text and JSON), and an edit session: three commands that make -02 with --output, checked, diffed. The point the owner made: each edit touches only the nodes it names, so a large draft is never rewritten by hand or by a language model.

section.p: Deletes examples/xquery/ and examples/xquery-project/.

section.title: 4. Transforming with XSLT (book-8) — examples: spec

item.p: xslt.md: built-in rules (the draft's text falls out), copying with changes (an identity transform that drops crefs for publication).

xslt-templates.md: template rules for the draft to HTML (section to section with h2, t, xref to links, bcp14 to <span class="bcp14">), text value templates, priorities (a requirement t vs a plain t), modes (toc for the table of contents; text for RFC-style plain text with 72-column lines and [RFC2119] references), starting elsewhere (--initial-template, --initial-mode).

xslt-keys-grouping.md: keys (xsl:key name="anchor": xref text computed from the target: "Section 4", "[RFC5234]", the term), numbers (xsl:number level="multiple" for section numbers, requirement numbers in document order), grouping (the term index grouped by first letter; references by normative/informative), sorting (references by anchor, with a collation pointer to Chapter 13).

xslt-packages.md: many outputs (one HTML page per top-level section with xsl:result-document and --result-directory), importing (common.xsl with the numbering and xref text, imported by html.xsl and text.xsl), functions (spec:number, spec:xref-text), packages (spec.xsl as a package used by both), transformations from queries (fn:transform from the XQuery index). One sentence says streaming is taught in Streaming Large Trace Files.

xslt-project.md, Project: Publishing the Specification: one script (publish.sh): validate, check.xq from Chapter 3 (symlink or a copy named publish-check.xq; book-8 must not depend on book-7's files unless book-7 has committed them: use only seed files and its own), HTML with the toc and the requirements index, the plain-text draft, a JSON requirements file for tools; and a "what changed" HTML page from both drafts (requirements marked added and changed).

section.p: Deletes examples/xslt/ and moves streaming (below).

section.title: 5. Project: Drawing Diagrams with SVG (book-10) — examples: svg

item.p: svg.md: what SVG is (an XML vocabulary in its namespace; boxes, text, lines, markers, style), diagram.xml and diagram.svg side by side, the plan.

svg-layout.md: the layout in XQuery: ranks by breadth-first distance as a fold over passes or a while clause (maps id to rank), rows with group by into arrays, positions as a map of records (declare record place(x, y)), the widest row, centring: maps, arrays, records, higher-order functions used for real.

svg-xquery.md: writing SVG with constructors: declare default element namespace, attributes from expressions, {{/}} in the style text, computed constructors for the shape by kind, output declarations (indent), --output=diagram.svg and diff against the committed file; draw.xqm (namespace urn:example:draw, draw:svg($diagram as element(diagram)) as element(), honouring the class attributes) is the reusable module other chapters link to. It must be committed early: Chapters 7, 11 and 12 use it.

svg-xslt.md: the same drawing with XSLT from a laid-out diagram (the XQuery adds x and y): template rules per element, a mode per layer (edges, nodes, labels), xsl:next-match for stores, attribute value templates, xpath-default-namespace for matching SVG.

svg-transform.md: transforming SVG files, any SVG: a dark theme (replace the style, identity with on-no-match="shallow-copy"), highlighting one node and its edges (a parameter), removing ids and metadata, listing the text of a drawing, scaling with viewBox; namespaces in patterns.

section.title: 6. Validating with XSD (book-9)

item.p: xsd.md (spec): the schema for the draft, validating both drafts, rules across values (the docName assertion), strict and lax, DTDs (xml2rfc's own DTD exists: one sentence; a two-line internal subset).

xsd-simple-types.md (spec): built-in types (gYear, positiveInteger), restriction with pattern, enumeration and range facets (draft-name, keyword, day), lists and unions (fragment schemas the packet adds: levels.xsd for a list of keywords, a union of day and a token), what validation does to values (whitespace in bcp14, typed values), facets that don't fit.

xsd-complex-types.md (spec): the schema read top-down; element declarations, sequence/choice/all (front, a section's blocks), attributes (use, fixed version), four kinds of content (empty date, simple title, element-only front, mixed t), mistakes in content, groups.

xsd-derivation.md (spec): extension (title and sourcecode extend xs:string; a requirement type extending text with a required anchor), restriction, xsi:type, substitution groups (block elements as a group: t, dl, sourcecode), nil (an empty day), block and final.

xsd-namespaces.md (scxml): a target namespace (SCXML's), namespace mistakes, xs:import of latch-data.xsd, ##other wildcards and lax processing (the XHTML inside states is not validated, the latch attributes are), schema hints (--use-schema-location), namespaces in queries.

xsd-identity.md (scxml): state ids as xs:key, targets and initial as xs:keyref, event names as xs:unique, paths in constraints (namespaced selectors), keys or IDs (and why latch.xsd uses xs:unique: most paragraphs have no anchor), broken copies the packet adds (bad-target.scxml, duplicate-event.scxml).

xsd-11.md (scxml): assertions on values and on elements (the status payload, data's one-of rule, a transition's event/cond/target), conditional type assignment (xs:alternative on latch:event by payload), open content, default attributes, xs:override (SCXML's full rule: a target list, xs:list of NCName, and what keyref then cannot check), smaller changes.

xsd-errors.md (spec): the parts of a message, errors in the schema, errors in documents (the broken drafts the packet adds: bad-keyword.xml, bad-anchor.xml, bad-xref.xml), after an element that is not allowed, not well-formed, lax, --format=json.

xsd-typed-data.md (scxml): typed values in XQuery (import schema, validate, data(@latch:type) as xs:QName, @expr as xs:string and the FORG0006 it gives in sum), values of your own types (latch:seconds), the xsi:type check of each data value, elements without a typed value, types in signatures (schema-element(latch:status)), typed copies, schema-aware XSLT, from C and JavaScript (pointers).

section.p: Deletes examples/xsd/.

section.title: 7. Project: Self-Describing State Machines (book-9) — examples: scxml

item.p: scxml.md: SCXML in one page (states, transitions, events, data model), the lock machine, its annotations (events with payload types, typed data, XHTML, latch:implements), validating it with both schemas.

scxml-checks.md: what the schema cannot check, as a schema-aware query check.xq: unreachable states (the closure of targets from initial, a while clause or fold), events handled but not declared, declared but unused (counting send and raise), payload names that name no element declaration, data values against their types (xsi:type and validate in try/catch), requirements implemented: latch:implements anchors that the draft does not have, and the draft's MUST requirements no state implements (scxml/latch.xml symlink to the seed). The four flaws of the seed are found; a fixed lock-fixed.scxml is made with an update (transition with) and checked clean.

scxml-xhtml.md: an XSLT document.xsl writing an XHTML page: the states with their XHTML copied through (xsl:copy-of with namespaces), a table of transitions, the events with their payload described from latch-data.xsd (doc("latch-data.xsd"): element children, types, facets as words, xs:documentation), links to the draft's requirements (latch.html#req-7). method xhtml.

scxml-drawing.md: the machine as diagram.xml (states as nodes, transitions as edges labelled with events; cycles, hence breadth-first ranks) drawn with ../svg/draw.xqm (symlink). Order: after book-10 has committed svg/draw.xqm.

section.title: 8. Parsing Text with Invisible XML (book-8 for one section)
section.p: Unchanged, except ixml-tasks.md gains a task "The grammar in a specification": the ABNF of latch.xml (symlink ixml/latch.xml) extracted with XPath and parsed with a small iXML grammar for ABNF rules (rule names, alternatives, repetitions), listing the rules each rule uses and the undefined ones (SP, CRLF, ALPHA, DIGIT come from RFC 5234's core rules). The performance chapter's numbers stay tied to tests/bench/run-ixml-bench.py --check and are not touched.

section.title: 9. JSON, CSV and HTML (book-12) — examples: traces
section.p: JSON with json-doc("before.json"): the lookup operator through resourceSpans, scopeSpans and spans, ?*, a filter on ?kind = 2, numbers become doubles and why OTLP writes times and int64 values as strings (xs:integer of startTimeUnixNano), json-to-xml of an OTLP file and xml-to-json; CSV: the spans as CSV for a spreadsheet (method=csv) and parse-csv of a CSV a tracing UI exports (a small spans.csv the packet adds); HTML: parse-html of a status page (status.html, added). The iXML section becomes one paragraph pointing to Chapter 8.

section.title: 10. Source Code as XML (book-11)
section.p: Unchanged (its small examples are about the bridge, not the library data); one sentence at the end points to the call-chain project.

section.title: 11. Project: A Diff of Call Chains (book-11) — examples: call-chains

item.p: call-chains.md: the lock service, the change in prose, the two directories, the plan.

call-chains-graph.md: functions (function_declaration, methods, and arrows assigned to consts), calls (call_expression and its function field), resolving callees: namespace imports (registry.getDoor to module registry), named imports (listDoors from ./doors.ts), local functions, and everything else as external (fetch, JSON.parse, doors.push is a method of a local, filtered); the graph as XML (<call from="doors.listDoors" to="registry.getDoor" line="20" repeated="true"/>, repeated when an ancestor is a loop); with --allow-file-access and file:list over before/ and after/.

call-chains-diff.md: chains from the entry points (server.route, server.start) to the leaves, made without recursion by a loop over a worklist (a while clause or fold) and with recursion (both correct; the book can show a recursive function here), the diff of edges and of chains (added, removed, now repeated), a text report and an HTML report, and the diff as diagram.xml with classes drawn by ../svg/draw.xqm (symlink; after book-10 commits it). The report ends with the prediction the traces will check: one call to the registry becomes one plus one per door.

section.title: 12. Project: Comparing Traces Before and After a Change (book-12) — examples: traces

item.p: traces.md: what a trace, a span, a resource and a scope are; OTLP JSON; the two files; the plan.

traces-tree.md: flattening resourceSpans into span records (for member, declare record span), a map from span id to span, the tree from parent ids, durations from nanosecond strings, the tree as XML (<span service="…" name="…" duration="…"> nested): the normal form the later sections and the streaming section use (trace.xqm).

traces-cardinality.md: participants from client spans (the server span's service, else server.address), grouping by (route, caller, callee), counts as a map; windows (taught here, all of the old section): tumbling windows over a span's children in start order to find runs of the same call (the N+1 as a run of four GET /doors/{id}), windows with an end, sliding windows (calls in any 20 ms), choosing between them.

traces-diff.md: the diff of two cardinality maps (added and removed participants, changed counts, the service versions), matching traces by root route, errors when files share no route (a typed error); the output above, as text and JSON.

traces-rendering.md: an HTML report (XSLT over the diff as XML: a table with added/removed rows and the counts) and the participants as a diagram.xml with added/removed/changed classes, drawn with ../svg/draw.xqm (symlink; after book-10 commits it).

traces-streaming.md: all of the old xslt-streaming.md, on traces: a query writes a large trace archive in the normal form (make-traces.xq --param=count=100000), a streamable mode counting spans per service, what can stream (the XTSE3430 example), accumulators (count per participant and the slowest span), xsl:iterate with xsl:break (the first trace slower than a threshold), more streaming (source-document, fork, merge of two archives by time), memory numbers measured again. Deletes examples/xslt-streaming/.

section.title: 13. Working with Text (book-8) — examples: spec
section.p: Collations (author and reference names, M'Raihi, sorted with the UCA collation; terms), full-text search over requirements ("lock" with stemming finds "locks" and "locked"; phrases; ftand; scores), dates in other languages (the draft's date with format-date in German and French, and the date built from year, month, day), numbers in words (format-integer(3, "w") checks that the text says "three"). Deletes examples/text/.

section.title: 14. Files and the Outside World (book-8) — examples: spec

section.title: 15. Embedding sxml in C (book-8) — examples: c

File names change (requirements.c for books.c).

section.title: 16. sxml in JavaScript (book-12) — examples: javascript, requires javascript
section.p: The same sections with traces/before.json (symlink) and the draft (symlink): processors and values, XQuery over OTLP JSON, XSLT and XSD on the draft, resources and errors, code languages unchanged, large outputs and inputs with a generated trace archive.

section.title: 17. Performance and Memory (book-12) — examples: traces
section.p: Build a release; compile once; lazy sequences (the first slow span of a large archive); look up instead of searching: parent lookup by scanning all spans vs a map by span id (the old slow-join/fast-join, now slow-tree.xq and fast-tree.xq over make-traces.xq's output); memory; the step limit; habits. The single chapter schematron.md, built on an invoice, becomes the part "Checking Rules with Schematron" after the state-machine project, on the Vane story: where Schematron fits beside XSD and XQuery, and how to write, run and embed it. The book never names invoices or their standards.
